catalog_quote: Like some of its neighboring languages, Indus Kohistani has pitch accent, i.e. one high tone per word. On long vowels and on short vowels followed by sonorants, the pitch accent is perceived as either rising or falling, depending on whether the accent is on the first or second mora. In this paper I follow Zoller (2005) in that a rising tone is represented with an acute accent as in á and aá, and a falling tone with a grave accent as in à and àa.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Lexical (mora-based) pitch accent: every word carries exactly one high-pitched accent on one mora; its location is a lexical property (not derivable by a positional rule - Bashir 2004 reporting Zoller 2005: 'the occurrence of rising or falling pitch is not predictable'; Baart 2003: Shina-type, 'stress is assigned to one of the moras of the word'). On bimoraic nuclei (long vowels, short V + sonorant) accent on the 2nd mora surfaces as rising (á, aá), on the 1st mora as falling (à, àa). Certain suffixes attract the accent (imperative -á, converb -eé), clitics such as =lee, loo are accentless (Lubberger 2014 pp. 25, 170).
new_statements.secondary_stress: None mentioned; 'one high tone per word'.
new_statements.exceptions: Accent shifts to some suffixes (kar- 'do' > kar-á 'do!'); enclitics lee/loo never bear or attract accent; particle -ãĩ takes over a word-final rising accent from its host (Lubberger 2012 p. 3; 2014 pp. 25, 170).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level lexical accent in citation forms; author is a fieldworker on the Pattan-area variety and explicitly adopts Zoller's (2005, Jijal variety) two-accent analysis and notation. The fuller primary analysis (Zoller 2005: 22-26ff; Hallberg & Hallberg 1999) could not be opened.
new_statements.identity_note: Lubberger's data are from the Pattan-area (west-bank Indus Kohistani proper, indu1241); she adopts the analysis and notation of Zoller 2005, whose dictionary is based on the Jijal variety; Hallberg & Hallberg 1999 used Seo and Jijal data. Buddruss 1959 describes Kanyawali (Tangir), a Maiyã outlier. Not to be confused with Kohistani Shina (Schmidt & Kohistani 2008; kohi1248/plk) or Kalam Kohistani (kala1373), which have different prosodic systems.

sources.citation: Lubberger, Beate. 2014. A description and analysis of four metarepresentation markers of Indus Kohistani. MA thesis, University of North Dakota. xiv+221 pp.
sources.note: fn. 7 p. 8: 'Indus Kohistani has pitch accent which is perceived as either rising or falling', notation after Zoller 2005; p. 170: 2sg imperative suffix -a attracts the root accent (kar-á 'do!'); converb -eé accented on last mora; clitics lee/loo have no accent of their own; refers reader to Hallberg 1999, Zoller 2005, Buddruss 1959 for phonology.

sources.note: Offprint p. 6: Indus Kohistani classed as 'Shina-type' (two surface tones, high-falling vs low-rising), 'based on as yet unpublished work on Indus Kohistani tone by Claus Peter Zoller, corroborated by some preliminary investigations of my own'; pp. 9-10: in Shina-type languages 'underlyingly, only stress is marked, and the relevant domain for stress is the mora' - stress is assigned (lexically) to one mora, H associates to it. Partly second-hand.
